did_you_know.text: Did you know? Reuben was Israel’s firstborn by birth, but after he defiled his father’s bed, the birthright was given to Joseph’s sons.

Did you know? This chapter distinguishes between three positions: Judah was powerful among his brothers and became their leader, Joseph received the birthright, and Reuben remained the firstborn in order of birth.
Did you know? Beerah, who was a leader of the Reubenites, was exiled by Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria.
Did you know? The Reubenites lived east of the Jordan, as far as the Euphrates, and the text explains that they needed extensive pasture because they had so many herds.
Did you know? The Gadites were recorded in genealogical registers during the reigns of Jotham, king of Judah, and Jeroboam, king of Israel.
Did you know? Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh fielded an army of 44,760 warriors, equipped with shields and swords, trained to use bows, and experienced in battle.
Did you know? According to the chapter, the Transjordan tribes’ victory over the Hagrites was attributed to their crying out to God and trusting in him.
Did you know? Half the tribe of Manasseh lived in the region of Bashan, extending to Baal-hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon, and the text notes that their descendants became numerous there.

Did you know? After the Transjordan tribes were unfaithful to the God of their ancestors and worshiped the gods of the peoples of the land, they were exiled by the kings of Assyria to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river of Gozan.
Did you know? The genealogy of the priests ends with Jehozadak, who went into exile when Judah and Jerusalem were taken into exile by Nebuchadnezzar.
